events.title: Blow for consumers as UK shop prices rise at fastest rate for two years
events.summary: Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in Prices for tech products also increased over the month as chip and memory shortages linked to the AI boom impacted the sector Your support helps us to tell the story From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. British consumers have been hit by the fastest-growing prices in two years, new data shows, as the cost of living continues to bite in the wake of the Iran war and tech-related payment surges. UK shop price inflation reached its highest level for two years in August, as accelerating food costs pressed on consumer budgets. Prices for tech products also increased over the month as chip and memory shortages linked to the AI boom impacted the supply and cost of electricals. British Retail Consortium (BRC)-NIQ figures showed that shop prices are now 1.5 per cent higher than a year ago, lifting from a rise of 0.9 per cent in July. The latest increase represents the sharpest rise since February 2024, when it was reported at 2.5 per cent for the month. Wider CPI inflation published by the Office for National Statistics sits at 2.9 per cent , though is expected to rise higher across the remainder of 2026, with the energy price cap having also seen another uplift last week. The BRC data shows non-food items rose 0.9 per cent, well above the three-month average of 0.6 per cent, but it was food and fresh food prices which continued to grow much faster - food inflation up to 2.8 per cent year on year, and fresh food at 3.0 per cent. That said, fresh food’s price increase rate is slightly down from July’s 3.1 per cent, and in line with a rolling three-month average. It comes after a recent uptick in wider inflation as spikes in oil and gas prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East pass through into energy costs for businesses and households. Experts linked the acceleration to higher energy costs in supply chains and the end of summer promotions and discounting. Fresh food inflation slowed slightly to 3 per cent, while the price rises for ambient foods increased to 2.5 per cent year-on-year. Inflation on products other than food also increased, rising to a two-year-high of 0.9 per cent for the month. This was significantly linked to an increase in the cost of technology, such as laptops, as soaring demand for memory driven by the AI industry increased costs for tech manufacturers. Helen Dickinson , chief executive of the BRC, said: “Shop price inflation rose to its highest level in over two years, albeit well below the headline Consumer Price Index. “The impact of higher energy, input and commodity costs is beginning to filter through into prices, particularly for ambient foods which are typically imported and processed. “In non-food, electrical prices rose amid the ongoing AI boom, which is forcing up the price of memory chips and storage.” Mike Watkins, head of retailer and business insight at NIQ, said: “While the increase in both food and non-food inflation is not unexpected, particularly as some of the summer promotional activity seen in recent months comes to an end, retailers continue to keep prices low, helping consumers manage rising household costs such as energy and fuel. “However, pressures are continuing to build across supply chains, and we can expect price competition to intensify as we move into the autumn months.” Join thought-provoking conversations, follow other Independent readers and see their replies Our Products Register Newsletters Donate Today’s Edition Install our app Archive Other publications International editions Independent en Español Independent Arabia Independent Turkish Independent Persian Independent Urdu The Standard Extras Puzzles All topics Free bets offers Latest deals Competitions and offers Independent Advertising Independent Ignite Syndication Working at The Independent Legal Code of conduct and complaints Contributors Cookie policy Donations Terms & Conditions Privacy policy User policies Modern Slavery Statement

events.title: Ikea invests $1.8 billion in Europe price cuts to lure cautious consumers
events.summary: Shoppers at the warehouse section of an Ikea store on the outskirts of Stockholm, Sweden. Ikea is investing €1.2 billion (S$1.77 billion) in Europe to cut prices and attract shoppers amid rising living costs and declining furniture sales. Price cuts affect over 1,500 products in key markets like Germany and Britain to make items more affordable. Ikea is redesigning products, increasing automation and opening smaller stores to reduce costs and better serve customers. LONDON – Swedish budget furniture retailer Ikea announced a new wave of price cuts on Sept 1 as it tries to boost demand in Europe, at a time when the surging cost of housing in many countries has dented people’s ability to move and curbed spending on furniture and homeware. Ikea said it was investing €1.2 billion ( S$1.77 billion ) in price cuts in total, with the aim of attracting cash-strapped shoppers and driving sales after two consecutive years of declining revenue. “The cost of living is increasing and it’s getting tougher and tougher for many people,” said Juvencio Maeztu, chief executive of Ingka, the biggest Ikea retailer worldwide, which operates Ikea stores in most European countries under the franchise model run by Inter Ikea, the brand owner and furniture supplier. “For many people, home is a bedroom in a shared house, and it’s even more important to offer storage and organised solutions,” he added. In Germany, Ikea’s biggest market by revenue, the retailer said it cut prices on more than 1,500 products, like the Poang chair reduced to €119 from €179. In Britain, the Kallax shelving unit was reduced to £49 (S$84) from £60 and the Alex drawer unit to £55 from £70. “We try to constantly optimise the cost picture by redesigning the products from the beginning,” said Jakub Jankowski, CEO of Inter Ikea, which sources from its own factories as well as third-party suppliers. A redesign of the Pax wardrobe line cut packaging costs by 70 per cent, he said. Greater automation and using renewable energy have also helped bring costs down, Jankowski said. Europe is a key manufacturing region for Ikea, with Poland, Italy, Lithuania and Germany among its top sourcing countries. As it tries to attract new customers, Ikea has also opened seven smaller stores across Europe since January, shifting away from its traditional out-of-town big-box model. Inter Ikea said its other franchisees had also agreed to price cuts: Sarton Group in the Balearic and Canary islands, Mapa in Turkey, Housemarket in Greece, Cyprus and Bulgaria, Miklatorg Group in Iceland and Inter Ikea Retail in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. events.title: Inquiry slams years of government failure before rushed fishing ban
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Inquiry finds years of mismanagement in lead up to Tasmania's sand flathead fishing ban The Tasmanian government banned the fishing of sand flathead in the state's south-east in March, due to dwindling stock numbers. ( Rick Stuart-Smith/Reef Life Survey ) The Tasmanian government banned people from fishing sand flathead across a large part of the state's south in March, due to numbers being critically depleted. An inquiry into that decision has found multiple issues with how the fishery was managed over the years and how the ban was handled. Among the recommendations is a call for the state government to publish what criteria would need to be met for the ban to be reversed. An inquiry into the ban on fishing sand flathead in Tasmania's south-east has found the state government failed to properly manage the species for years, before rushing through the ban. Sand flathead are a brown, ray-finned fish found at the bottom of inshore waters across all of Tasmania, as well as a very popular target for the state's recreational fishers. In March, the state government imposed a ban on fishing the species across a large part of Tasmania's south, between Whale Head and Cape Pillar, due to a severe decline in stock. A lower house committee, which was formed to scrutinise the fishery closure decision following frustration from the community, tabled its report in parliament on Tuesday. The new rules around catching sand flathead came into effect from March 1. ( Fishing Tasmania ) It handed down a range of findings and criticisms of the state government, but it did not explicitly state that the decision to close the fishery was incorrect. The committee found there was a consensus that the south-east sand flathead fishery was "under pressure" and the "precautionary principle" was employed in the decision to close it. However, it also found the state government had failed to quickly act on scientific advice about the species over several years, contributing to its ongoing deterioration. Gavin Pearce, the state's primary industries minister, told the inquiry in June that the decision to close the fishery was "not taken lightly" and was necessary to "support recovery of the stock". "The south-east stock is critically depleted — with around only 1 per cent of fish above the legal size limit and breeding potential reduced significantly to very low levels," he said. In its submission to the inquiry, the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies said it determined that too many sand flatheads were being fished more than a decade ago. "Stock assessment modelling began in 2014–15 and immediately determined that long-term fishing mortality has exceeded levels consistent with sustainability targets," it said. Gavin Pearce told the inquiry the dwindling number of sand flathead had been known for a "long period". ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) The committee also heard that the species was classed as "depleting" in a 2016 report and that this was upgraded to "depleted" in 2021. "In terms of this being a new thing that just suddenly snuck up on us, well, it didn't," Mr Pearce told the inquiry. The inquiry found fishery closures were "reflective of a failure in long-term planning and management". 'Perfunctory' consultation criticised The inquiry also found there was a lack of consultation with the community and stakeholders about the closure, which "raised concerns about the decision-making process". In its submission, the Department of Natural Resources and Environment (NRE) said relevant fishing bodies were contacted in February and given a consultation period of about two weeks. Multiple stakeholders, including both TARFish and RecFishTas, told the inquiry they were only able to provide feedback on the closure after it had already been announced by Mr Pearce. "Attempts [to] consult occurring after the decision has been made, is merely perfunctory, and cannot inform or impact on the decision," TARFish said in its submission to the inquiry. The committee found there was a lack of consultation with the community and stakeholders about the closure. ( ABC News ) The inquiry also found that the state government did not model the economic impact of closing the sand flathead fishery and that this had still not been done. It also found the decision-making processes undertaken by Mr Pearce and NRE created confusion for the community, which was worsened by inconsistency in public details.

events.title: Foreign investors expected to eye more China A shares – but pace set to ease: analyst
events.summary: Overseas capital in yuan-traded Chinese stocks faces cooling, as tech sentiment, US yields and yuan strength steer the next phase “We still expect net inflows in the second half, but the pace will be somewhat slower than in the first half,” said Meng Lei, China equity strategist at UBS Securities, at UBS’s annual China A-share strategy conference in Shenzhen on Tuesday. Foreign appetite for A shares – domestic shares of mainland companies denominated and traded in yuan – hit a record in the first half. Overseas holdings reached more than 4.4 trillion yuan (US$654 billion) by the second quarter, the highest level on record, according to Meng. However, analysts said several macroeconomic headwinds were tempering foreign capital inflows into onshore bourses.

events.title: Brisbane's ferry workers to go on strike during Riverfire
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Brisbane ferry workers to undertake 24-hour Riverfire work stoppage amid pay dispute with CityCat operator Brisbane's CityCats will remain in their docks for Riverfire as ferry workers undetake industrial action. ( ABC News: Dean Caton ) Brisbane ferry workers will undertake a 24-hour work stoppage on Saturday, coinciding with the Riverfire annual fireworks display. Pay negotiations between the Maritime Union of Australia (MUA) and RiverCity Ferries have been ongoing since October last year, with workers conducting industrial action intermittently since July 30. About half-a-million people are expected to travel to river precincts for Riverfire on Saturday, with 27,000 people using CityCats and ferries last year. Attendees at Brisbane's Riverfire will have to grapple with transport woes this weekend, as ferry workers confirm they will stop work for 24 hours on Saturday. The Maritime Union of Australia (MUA) said its latest industrial action will fall on Saturday, the same day as Brisbane's annual fireworks display. It's the latest episode in a long-running pay dispute between MUA and RiverCity Ferries, which runs ferry and CityCat services along the Brisbane River in partnership with the Brisbane City Council (BCC). The Maritime Union of Australia has been in pay negotiations with operator RiverCity Ferries since October last year. ( ABC News: Giulio Saggin ) Workers will walk off the job at 4am on Saturday morning. Pay negotiations between the parties have been taking place since October last year, and MUA ferry workers have been undertaking work stoppages of varying lengths since July 30. The BCC has condemned the move to conduct the action on the day of Riverfire. Up to half a million people are expected to travel to major precincts along the river on Saturday evening for the Riverfire display, which officially opens the Brisbane Festival. About 27,000 people used Brisbane ferry services to travel to Riverfire last year. About half-a-million people are expected to travel to river precincts for Riverfire on Saturday. ( ABC News: Christopher Gillette ) General manager of RiverCity Ferries Paul Rigby said the union was planning to "spoil the party". "Riverfire is one of the biggest nights on the Brisbane calendar, a time for family and friends to come together and celebrate along the waterway that shapes and serves the city," he said. Mr Rigby called on the union to scrap the planned action. "We value our hard-working staff and have worked to put a strong offer on the table for them. "But unions are planning to spoil the party and disrupt the plans of tens of thousands of travellers for the sake of their protracted and unreasonable industrial campaign." MUA organiser Jaiden Simpson said the union acknowledged council's concerns about the timing but denied council allegations it was trying to "ruin" Riverfire. "We would deny that wholeheartedly, and in fact I would say that RiverCity Ferries haven't meaningfully engaged with the unions or the delegates or their workforce for the past 17 meetings," Mr Simpson said. He said the union had a range of concerns that had not been addressed by the operator. "Fatigue management, work-life balance, meal break provisions, obviously salary and superannuation are to be addressed, but a range of other conditions RiverCity Ferries has chosen not to address at all," he said. Jaiden Simpson says RiverCity Ferries proposed an offer to workers that wasn't endorsed by the MUA. ( ABC News: Lottie Twyford ) Mr Simpson said the latest offer was equal to the Fair Work Commission's annual wage increase. He said the MUA is seeking a three-year agreement with a six per cent pay rise in the first year, with subsequent increases yet to be decided on. In a statement, BCC's chair for public transport Andrew Wines criticised what he described as "a stunt designed to cause maximum pain". Andrew Wines says the planned industrial action is "an absolute disgrace". ( ABC News ) "Riverfire is one of Brisbane's biggest nights of the year and it's an absolute disgrace the union is planning to mess with it," Councillor Wines said. He said the union hadn't given members time to vote on the latest offer by RiverCity Ferries. Mr Simpson rejected that claim, and said members voted for strike action after RiverCity Ferries last week put out an offer that wasn't endorsed by the union for voting to open this weekend. "We haven't chosen to do this lightly, and our membership in the union does not want to … proceed with this industrial action," Mr Simpson said.

events.title: Boss of City regulator accused of threatening consumer group over £9.1bn car loan scheme
events.summary: FCA chief, Nikhil Rathi, warned of ‘adverse consequences’ if challenge made to settlement, court filings allege The boss of the UK’s financial regulator is accused of threatening a consumer group with “adverse consequences” if it blocked a £9.1bn compensation scheme meant to settle the motor finance scandal . Legal documents reviewed by the Guardian said the alleged comments by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) chief executive, Nikhil Rathi, amounted to “an inappropriate intervention by a public official”. The threat is said to have taken place during a Microsoft Teams call with the directors of Consumer Voice (CV) on 27 April, hours before the deadline to file legal challenges against the FCA’s proposed redress scheme for those missold car loans. Rathi warned that the City regulator would be “unable to collaborate” with Consumer Voice if it took legal action, “suggesting adverse consequences for CV’s future engagement with the FCA and adverse press briefings against it”, the filings said. “The implication was clear: the FCA’s willingness to engage constructively with CV was contingent on CV not challenging the scheme, and would give way to hostility if it did,” the documents claimed. Up until that point, the FCA had treated Consumer Voice as a “trusted expert consumer body”, the filings said. But once the group decided to challenge the scheme, “the FCA changed its position … now the FCA seeks to denigrate CV’s activities and motives in bringing this application”. Rathi also allegedly claimed that their potential legal challenge was the “biggest risk to the scheme” and that plans to get money to millions of victims by this Christmas would fail if directors followed through with their plans. The filings say it was not disclosed that three specialist lenders were also planning to challenge the scheme, only that the FCA had been “engaging with the banks”, who, over the previous weekend, decided not to challenge the payout plan. The episode marks a fresh controversy in the long-running saga surrounding mis-sold UK car loans, which prompted a contentious intervention by former chancellor Rachel Reeves last year, following intense lobbying by big banks. Lenders have been arguing that a large compensation bill would risk spooking investors and causing long-lasting economic damage to the UK. The documents were filed at the UK’s upper tribunal, as part of the wider legal challenge against the terms of the FCA’s compensation scheme. Consumer Voice and the specialist lenders – Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes-Benz Financial Services and Crédit Agricole Auto Finance – are challenging the scheme on different grounds. Consumer Voice, founded by former Which? staffers Nikki Stopford and Alex Neill in 2023, is the only group arguing for bigger compensation for drivers who were overcharged as a result of lenders paying out commission to car dealerships between 2007 and 2024. They say the scheme is low-balling consumers – offering average payouts of £830 per mis-sold loan – and is putting the interests of profit-making lenders, who fear big bills, ahead of the interests of consumers it is meant to protect. The FCA has since tried to get the claim by Consumer Voice thrown out of court by alleging that its co-founders have not been transparent about their funding and potential conflicts of interest. Last month, legal documents lodged by the regulator suggested Consumer Voice was not being honest about its business model and relationship with its lawyers at Courmacs Legal. Both firms, “operate for profit in the sphere of claims management”, the FCA said, adding that Courmacs had previously hired Consumer Voice to conduct consumer research on its behalf. The consumer group “therefore has commercial incentives of its own”. Consumer Voice says it partners with law firms with an aim to help consumers “get back money they’re owed from rule-breaking companies”. It has promoted claims against the likes of Amazon, Facebook, Mastercard, Apple iCloud, and Sony PlayStation, and makes money by doing communications work for law firms to raise awareness of their claims. It also receives a commission when its members join one of the law firms’ cases, according to its website. Courmacs, based in Blackburn, says it is providing pro bono services in the case against the FCA. Ultimately, larger payouts for consumers will boost Courmacs’ earnings, with the firm taking up to 30% of client settlements. A spokesperson for the FCA said “we don’t recognise the way this conversation has been characterised”, adding that officials had spoken to a range of parties, including lenders and claims firms ahead of the deadline. “It was important to explain the implications for consumers and that we would defend the scheme robustly as the best way of getting compensation paid,” the FCA said. “We were also clear that we would be upfront with consumers about why expected compensation would be delayed.

events.title: What happened to Shein? Shares slide in fast-fashion retailer’s Hong Kong debut
events.summary: Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in Known globally for selling $5 tops and $10 dresses, Shein was founded in China in 2012 Your support helps us to tell the story From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. The online fast-fashion retailer has been humbled by tariff and duty changes in the U.S. and Europe that have contributed to a dramatic decline in valuation for the company . Known globally for selling $5 tops and $10 dresses, Shein was founded in China in 2012 and has been headquartered in Singapore since late 2021. The retailer has spent years touting its credentials as a global company before re-embracing its Chinese roots to list in Hong Kong. That capped a four-year quest to go public after failing to list in New York and London. Intense scrutiny of its business practices also hampered its attempts that were ultimately blocked by Chinese authorities. Its shares traded at HK$46.62 by mid-session, down from its HK$48.56 IPO price but recovering somewhat from an earlier slide of as much as 10 per cent. That values the company at about $25.3 billion, compared to its peak of nearly $100 billion in 2022. "As a new company listed in Hong Kong, we will continue to innovate, optimise, and cooperate with our supply chain partners for mutual benefit and win-win results," Shein Chief Financial Officer Leigh Gui said at the opening gong ceremony. Founder and CEO Sky Xu, known for disliking the limelight, did not speak at the event, though later took pictures with Shein employees on stage. He declined to respond to questions. Investors and analysts have worried about Shein's slower growth, higher trade costs and tighter regulatory scrutiny. "I think the weak debut shows that even after the huge valuation reset, investors still don't see Shein as obviously cheap," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo. She said Shein was valued at 15 times forward earnings, more than double the multiple for PDD, the owner of rival Temu, which meant "investors were being asked to pay a premium despite weaker growth visibility and significant regulatory and trade risks." Demand for Shein's stock during the IPO was tepid compared to high-profile offerings from the AI and robotics sectors. The retail tranche was subscribed 5.63 times, while the international portion was subscribed 2.59 ​times. Some deals have been hundreds of times oversubscribed, especially from Hong Kong's army of retail investors who track IPOs very closely. Despite Shein's growth worries, existing investors who participated in the IPO included billionaire Michael Bloomberg's family office Willett Advisors, French billionaire entrepreneur and investor Xavier Niel, and Microsoft, a filing showed on Monday. Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Reliance also bought more shares in Shein, according to the filing, as did Bolivian American billionaire Marcelo Claure's Claure Group, and the SoftBank 9984.T Vision Fund. The amount sold in the IPO represents about 6.6 per cent of Shein's enlarged share capital. Cornerstone investors took about one-fifth of the IPO and are locked up for six months, leaving roughly 5 per cent freely tradeable. Last year, the U.S. ended the de minimis duty exemption for e-commerce shipments under $800 that had powered Shein's direct-shipping model. The European Union recently followed suit, imposing fees on low-value packages. Shein's net income slid 39 per cent last year and it swung to a loss in the first quarter. Shein has said it expects first-half operating profit margin to be slightly lower than in the first quarter, hurt by higher customs duties, tariffs, fees and logistics costs in Europe and the Middle East. "Daily active users in Europe have fallen around 45 per cent since the EU scrapped its duty exemption on small parcels, and Temu has seen a similar drop," said Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for Asia-Pacific at eToro. "This is less a Shein problem, but more so the end of an era for cheap cross-border shipping. The brand's reach is unquestionable, but a large share of that loyalty has always belonged to the price tag.

events.title: Crackdown on alleged misuse of housing contract sunset clauses in SA
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Topic: Housing Construction Industry Consumer and Business Affairs Minister Michael Brown says developers who misuse sunset clauses will soon face the full force of the law. ( ABC News: Daniel Taylor ) Legislation to stop homebuyers being left high and dry by developers misusing sunset clauses in contracts will soon be introduced to SA parliament. Under current arrangements, sunset clauses allow both parties to terminate contracts if homes are not completed by an agreed date, but can be misused — allegedly by developers who want to cash in on rising property values. The SA government says it will conduct consultation in the coming weeks and wants to introduce legislation to parliament by the end of the year. South Australian homebuyers could soon be protected from "sunset clauses" that allow housing developers to terminate contracts for off-the-plan properties, the state government says. The move comes after the government vowed to consider legislative options when a developer axed 75 contracts with homebuyers in Gawler East . Under current arrangements, sunset clauses allow developers as well as homebuyers to terminate contracts if homes are not completed by an agreed date. In some cases they can be misused — allegedly by developers who want to make a larger profit when property values increase . The SA government said it would introduce legislation to parliament by the end of the year to prevent developers from misusing the clauses. The proposed reforms would prevent a developer from triggering a sunset clause unless it had the consent of the homebuyer, or if the Supreme Court ruled that such a step was "just and equitable", the state government said. "They'll need to go to a court and ask the court to rule that it's appropriate they use the sunset clause," Consumer and Business Affairs Minister Michael Brown said. "The message we want to send to the developers is 'if you want to come to South Australia and develop and provide housing for people and, yes, make some money while you're doing it, then we're happy to work with you'. Homebuyers at Springwood Estate at Gawler East were plunged into uncertainty earlier this year. ( ABC News: Briana Fiore ) The move comes amid significant housing development across Adelaide, and follows similar steps in other states including New South Wales and Queensland. Mr Brown said its latest legislation push followed property developers Wel.Co axing 75 contracts at a Springwood Estate housing development in Gawler East. He said that while that particular situation had largely been "rectified", there was still a need to strengthen consumer protections. "It's unfortunate it took media attention and also the government to step in to get Wel.Co to end up where they did," he said. "That's one of the reasons why we're changing the legislation — to make sure we don't end up with a Wel.Co style problem again." In response, the developer said the situation at Springwood "arose following significant changes to planning and infrastructure requirements affecting the project". "These were complex circumstances, and Wel.Co has continued to work closely with government, council and affected purchasers to identify pathways forward," Wel.Co said. "Our focus remains on working constructively with all parties to achieve the best possible outcomes for purchasers and progress the delivery of Springwood." The minister said the government would conduct consultation in the coming weeks.

events.title: Former WeWork CEO's property company Flow hiring as it launches in the UAE
events.summary: Residential real estate company Flow, launched by WeWork co-founder Adam Neumann, aims to rapidly boost its workforce as it begins operations in the UAE. The company, which has its headquarters in the US and owns and operates properties, has received a commercial licence from the Dubai International Financial Centre , it said in a statement on Tuesday. "We’re in advanced negotiations for our first properties in the UAE and expect to open our first communities by [the first quarter of] 2027," said Arif Shah, chief executive of Flow UAE. Projects are planned in Abu Dhabi and Dubai. He confirmed that the company is recruiting as it builds up its team, having hired 10 people in the past three months. "At a time when some companies are being cautious on hiring, we’re doing the opposite. We’re establishing a global design and development centre of excellence in Dubai," Mr Shah said. It plans to open an experience centre in Al Quoz by December that will also serve as its design studio and Dubai office. The team in the Dubai is also to oversee and support Flow development projects globally, initially across the US and Saudi Arabia, he said. "We now have a team of 16 people based in Dubai and are continuing to recruit across a number of functions. We’ll likely be 40 to 50-strong by the end of the year," he added. Property investments up The UAE's property sector has continued to grow and attract investments despite the impact of the Iran war. Investments in completed real estate projects in Dubai jumped by more than half in the first half of 2026, state news agency Wam reported last month, quoting data from the Dubai Land Department . The total value of these developments in the six months through June hit Dh111 billion ($30.2 billion), up 52 per cent year-on-year from Dh73 billion in the same period in 2025. The UAE was also ranked as the world's leading real estate investment destination as the industry has been able to retain its momentum despite recent challenges, according to Arada's UAE Property Investment Index released in June. Flow was set up in 2021 with a $350 million investment from US venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z). It was set up by Adam Neumann, co-founder and former chief executive of WeWork, whose rapid expansion and unconventional corporate governance came under intense scrutiny during the office-sharing company's failed attempt to go public in 2019. Mr Neumann stepped down as chief executive that year as WeWork's valuation plunged and investors raised concerns about its losses, governance and his leadership. The SoftBank-backed company subsequently filed for bankruptcy protection in 2023. Flow entered Saudi Arabia in 2024 with the acquisition of about 1,000 units. It currently has a $2.5 billion portfolio, including 8,500 residences currently under management or in development, Flow said.

events.title: Nimbys can’t stand in the way of Labour’s legacy: a 21st-century new town boom | Polly Toynbee
events.summary: Nimbys can’t stand in the way of Labour’s legacy: a 21st-century new town boom Which do Enfield’s Tories and Greens value more – a golf course or thousands of new homes? It’s a question of political values N ew towns will again be a lasting Labour legacy, just as in the eras of Clement Attlee and Harold Wilson. Those monuments to optimism, created in the mid-20th century by pulling down slums and building better, will be joined by seven more in an attempt to ease the housing crisis. Enfield has been the exemplar, its proposed 21,000-home new town enthusiastically backed by its previous Labour council, which was struggling with 3,000 families expensively dumped into miserable temporary accommodation, and, I’m told, 7,000 on the waiting list. But in May’s elections, the great anti-Labour storm brought in a regime resisting the new town in every way it can. A minority Conservative group, propped up by the Greens (yes, Tory-backing Greens), informed the government that it was “withdrawing” . Both parties had run on an anti-new town campaign. Enfield council’s Tory leader, Alessandro Georgiou, gave me this quote, but no interview: “We were elected on a clear mandate to protect Enfield’s green belt, and we have honoured that commitment by formally withdrawing from the new town process.” But there is no “process”, as it was never in a council’s power to block a new town. Devolution and localism? Only so far. Major infrastructure of national importance can’t, won’t and shouldn’t be stopped by local nimbys. Extending the grid, new power generation, waste recycling, transport by rail, air or ports, reservoirs and water treatment would never happen without planning from above. Building a new town falls under the regional control of the mayor, who has oversight of the interests of a far wider population. The London mayor, Sadiq Khan, is faced with a desperate housing shortage . He has the say-so here, and strongly supports new town plans for Enfield and Thamesmead. But pleading the interests of unhoused people rather than the voters in their patch will get councillors unseated, which is why they’re always brandishing alternative plans for building elsewhere, not here. Enfield is the perfect borough for a new town, with excellent rail connections. Opponents protest that it is green belt land, but that’s not how much of it feels. Step out at Crews Hill station and all around is a cluster of glasshouses and garden centres, an unplanned sprawl. There is some charm in its haphazardness, but it is exactly what the government calls “grey belt” – technically green belt, but concreted over, one way or another. Chase Park, the other part of the plan, is described in government plans as “low-quality agricultural land”. I was taken round by Ergin Erbil, who was the Labour council leader until he was defeated in May. He understands housing need: he has just moved into a privately rented two-bedroom flat with his wife and children. “I’ve a degree, a reasonable job, but we’ll never afford to buy,” he tells me. He agrees with Khan’s office: when the mayor and the then housing minister Steve Reed last year proposed cutting the affordable housing quota for fast-tracked developments from 35% to 20%, one official said : “20% of something is better than 35% of nothing.” Local campaigners call Enfield London’s “green lungs”. But do golfing greens really count? Weirdly unnatural and often closed to the public, they are estimated to swallow billions of litres of water a year in England. The new town would mean building 5,500 homes over an area including Crews Hill golf club, to great protest from its members, who each pay up to £1,980 a year . Enfield has five other golf courses , part of a London “golf belt”. Weighing some green belt loss against gaining 21,000 homes goes to the heart of political values. Enfield’s Green councillors made their choice: by protesting against the new town, they gave the council to the Conservatives . New towns were always mocked by Tories for their New Jerusalem optimism. But the housing minister, Matthew Pennycook, tells me he has been speaking to planners from the last wave who can warn him of things they got wrong, and steer him towards what worked best. Don’t build them around the car, but rather public transport. Don’t build suburban garden cities when only high-density housing guarantees a big enough community to support frequent buses, busy shops, schools, clinics, leisure and new enterprises. Lack of civic planning failed to build enough housing for decades, while covering the countryside with isolated clumps of executive homes. Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more And these planners have proved themselves: after the contemptuous snobbery that greeted its birth almost 60 years ago, Milton Keynes has recently been declared one of the UK’s best places to live . Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

events.title: Sony and Warner Music sue Anthropic over alleged theft of ‘tens of thousands’ of songs, including ‘I Am the Walrus’ and ‘Hallelujah’
events.summary: Last month, Anthropic was at the center of public backlash for a plan , called Project Panama, to “destructively scan all the books in the world” to train its Claude AI models. Now the AI company finds itself again facing the (copyright) music. Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell Music have sued Anthropic, naming CEO Dario Amodei and cofounder Benjamin Mann as individual defendants, for what the suit characterizes as illegally downloading, scraping, and torrenting “thousands upon thousands” of copyrighted songs to train its AI models. The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Northern California, alleges that Anthropic obtained lyrics and sheet music through pirate sources including Library Genesis and the Pirate Library Mirror, and, according to the complaint, scraped licensed lyric websites, such as Musixmatch and LyricFind. The publishers allege the material was then incorporated into Claude’s training data and that the model can reproduce copyrighted lyrics. “In blatant violation of copyright law, Defendants have unlawfully acquired troves of Music Publishers’ musical compositions, and then systematically copied those works multiple times,” the filing read, “including as the inputs to train Anthropic’s Claude AI models and in the outputs those models generate.” Scraping and distributing Musixmatch content violates the site’s user agreement , and LyricFind’s privacy policy similarly prohibits reproduction “unless otherwise stated,” the suit says. Sony and Warner are seeking statutory damages of up to $150,000 for each song the court finds Anthropic to have infringed willfully. They are also seeking as much as $25,000 for each instance in which copyright-management information was allegedly removed from a work. With the complaint covering at least “thousands if not tens of thousands” of works, the potential damages could reach into the billions of dollars. Among the songs named in the complaint are Marvin Gaye and Tammi Terrell’s “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough,” Mariah Carey’s “All I Want for Christmas Is You,” Survivor’s “Eye of the Tiger,” Leonard Cohen’s “Hallelujah,” Mark Ronson and Bruno Mars’ “Uptown Funk,” the Beatles’ “I Am the Walrus,” and Taylor Swift’s “Paper Rings” and “Cruel Summer.” Anthropic rejected the allegations and said the company will “defend ourselves robustly” in court.  “This is the third lawsuit from the same lawyers, recycling allegations from cases already before the courts,” an Anthropic spokesperson told Fortune . It’s true that Anthropic has some history with the law firm: Oppenheim and Zebrak , which represents Sony and Warner in the new suit, first sued Anthropic in October 2023 alongside Universal Music Publishing Group, Concord Music Group, and ABKCO over roughly 500 songs. The same publishers filed a second suit through the same firm in January, covering more than 20,000 works and seeking over $3 billion. BMG and Round Hill Music have also sued Anthropic over music this year, but with different counsel—putting the total number of music-copyright suits against the company at five. Anthropic’s other copyright fights  Anthropic points to Bartz v. Anthropic as precedent for its fair use in using human-made work to train its models. The company says “training generative AI models is a transformative fair use—as the court held in Bartz ,” highlighting the judge’s ruling on the use of copyrighted works. “In short, the purpose and character of using copyrighted works to train LLMs to generate new text was quintessentially transformative,” Judge William Alsup wrote in June 2025 regarding the case. “Like any reader aspiring to be a writer, Anthropic’s LLMs trained upon works not to race ahead and replicate or supplant them—but to turn a hard corner and create something different.” The AI company settled in September 2025 for $1.5 billion with the owners of the copyrighted works. But Sony and Warner said it wasn’t enough. “Anthropic clearly considers that to be just the cost of doing business given that its entire business model continues to be built on copyright theft,” the new Sony and Warner complaint read. “And $1.5 billion is obviously not a large enough settlement to deter infringing conduct by a company that has parlayed such mass infringement into a staggering $2-trillion-dollar valuation,” the complaint stated, referencing Anthropic’s IPO target.  “In the process of building and operating AI models, Anthropic unlawfully copies and disseminates vast amounts of copyrighted works—including the lyrics to myriad musical compositions owned or controlled by Publishers,” the lawsuit filing read. Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell did not immediately respond to Fortune ‘s requests for comment. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

Fast fashion giant Shein has seen its shares slide after finally launching its stock market debut at a fraction of previous valuations of the company. However, they recovered some ground during the session to remain around 4% lower, at 46.36 Hong Kong dollars (£4.37). It had started the initial public offering (IPO) at a price of 48.56 Hong Kong dollars (£4.58), with a market value above 26 billion US dollars (£19.4 billion). This represents a significant slump in value of the business in recent years, having reportedly been worth more than 100 billion US dollars (£73.3 billion) at its peak after a private fundraising in 2022. It was said to have been initially aiming for a 30 billion US dollar (£22 billion) valuation. The drop in the retail firm’s value has come off the back of pressure from global tax changes and weak consumer sentiment. The Singapore-based online firm had been planning to float since 2023 and previous attempts to list in New York and London failed after political and regulatory scrutiny. Shein recently disclosed it slumped to a 99 million US dollar (£73 million) bottom line loss in the first quarter of 2026 and saw sales hit by US President Donald Trump’s move to scrap an import duty exemption on small packages. In May last year, the US removed a so-called “de minimis” tariff exemption on small packages, which Shein had previously used to ship garments from China directly to customers. Earlier this month, the European Union also made the same move by imposing a three euro (£2.56) duty on small parcels imported from outside the trading bloc. The UK is also planning to close the small parcels loophole, but not until October 2028. Shein said in the trading update it was looking at raising prices across the US and Europe to offset the sales impact. events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts No penalties for Chris Ellison, Mineral Resources as ASIC ends alleged tax evasion probe Chris Ellison addressed shareholders at Mineral Resources 2024 AGM. ( Supplied: Mineral Resources ) The Australian Securities and Investments Commission says it will not impose penalties against WA miner Mineral Resources and its billionaire boss Chris Ellison after an investigation into alleged tax evasion. MinRes has been under scrutiny after Mr Ellison failed to disclose a financial interest he held in an offshore company that was one of his suppliers. Separately, investors have filed a class action suit in Victoria's Supreme Court against Mr Ellison and the company. Western Australian mining billionaire Chris Ellison and his flagship company will face "no action" from the federal corporate regulator, which had been investigating Mineral Resources for alleged tax evasion. Mr Ellison and the Perth-based iron ore and lithium miner were under scrutiny from the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) after an internal review found he had failed to disclose a financial interest he held in an offshore company that sold almost $4 million worth of equipment to MinRes in the early 2000s. That company was based in the British Virgin Islands, a territory where companies do not pay income tax. In April 2025, the mining boss apologised and announced he would step down from his post as managing director, however there has been no announcement of his successor. ASIC today confirmed its investigation was finished, and that it would not impose penalties or other enforcement actions against Mr Ellison or MinRes. Mineral Resources' headquarters in Osborne Park, eight kilometres north west of Perth's CBD. ( ABC News ) "ASIC assessed the available evidence, applicable law, prospects of success and broader public interest considerations before determining that no further regulatory action was warranted," it said in a statement. Separately, investors have filed a class action against Mr Ellison and MinRes in Victoria's Supreme Court over the alleged tax scandal. In late 2024, Mineral Resources' board ordered Mr Ellison to pay $8.8 million in financial penalties, and decided not to pay almost $10 million in planned executive remuneration. Mr Ellison has apologised for the incident. ( Supplied: MinRes ) The board's internal investigation also found company funds had been used to benefit entities in which Mr Ellison's daughter had an interest, without Mineral Resources' knowledge. Mr Ellison told shareholders at the time he was deeply sorry for his actions. MinRes boss addresses angry shareholders on tax investigation Chris Ellison says an investigation into a corporate governance scandal gripping the mining company he founded almost 20 years ago is a "dark cloud over [his] life". "I made an error of judgement with reporting of personal tax. I deeply regret the impact this has had on our business and our people." Mr Ellison had also admitted to shareholders he had operated overseas entities and not disclosed revenue from these ventures. But he said the matter had since been settled, and all outstanding tax, penalties and interest had now been paid back.

events.title: Citigroup boosts headcount by 25% on north Asia desk, Invesco names new Asia-Pacific head
events.summary: US financial firms Citigroup and Invesco are continuing to expand in Asia even amid geopolitical uncertainties US financial institutions Citigroup and Invesco have separately announced that they would continue to expand their presence in Asia, even as the financial industry faces geopolitical uncertainties and Beijing tightens its control on overseas investment. Citi would boost the headcount of its north Asia and Japan corporate banking desk network by 25 per cent following double-digit growth in client activities, it said in a statement on Tuesday. The US lender would also expand its China desk network by adding Brazil and Europe as new hubs, on top of existing centres in Hong Kong, Singapore, Dubai, London, New York, San Francisco and South Africa. “The expansion supports the next phase of Chinese companies’ global growth ambitions as they move beyond low-cost manufactured exports and cross-border acquisitions to building hi-tech supply chain ecosystems overseas, focusing on AI infrastructure, electric vehicles, consumer electronics and green energy,” said Toh Jianxun, head of corporate banking at Citi for Japan, Asia North and Australia. US tariffs, the war in the Middle East and the war between Russia and Ukraine had created uncertainties but also led companies to seek diversification of their supply chain and trading partners, adding new opportunities for Citi and other financial firms, according to analysts. Citi, which operates across 90 countries, would add new investments across South America, Europe and parts of Asia to support the overseas expansion activities of Citi’s corporate clients headquartered in Japan, Korea, mainland China and Taiwan. The desks would offer cross-border financing, foreign exchange, payment and other trade services. “Citi is seeing strong client growth across a number of corridors connecting markets in North Asia and Japan with global markets. These investments underline our commitment to clients to invest further to support their growth and expansion,” Toh said.

The yield of the Australian government's 10-year bond has climbed to a 15-year high, in a worrying sign for Australian borrowers. The bond is an IOU, with the buyer of that particular bond receiving fixed payments for money lent to the Australian government for a decade, but now bonds are being sold off due to market concerns about inflation. Japanese, British and US government bond yields have also surged, demonstrating growing global concern about debt and inflation. The Australian government's 10-year bond yield has climbed to a 15-year high in a worrying sign for Australian borrowers. In afternoon trade, the interest rate on the bond was 5.16 per cent. The 10-year Australian Government bond yield rose to 5.16%, the highest level since April 2011. ( The Reserve Bank ) It reached 5.24 per cent in April 2011 before a steady decline until the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, when it began to climb from a low of 0.55 per cent. A bond is an IOU, with the buyer of a particular bond receiving fixed payments for money loaned to the Australian government for a decade. Now Australian bonds are being sold off because the market is concerned about inflation. Bonds lose their value as inflation expectations increase. So investors seek higher compensation for this by demanding a better interest rate on the bonds. The price of a bond and its yield move in opposite directions. So the lower bond prices fall, the higher its interest rate rises. This is a problem, says AMP's chief economist Shane Oliver, given Australia's gross national debt recently surpassed $1 trillion. Shane Oliver says rising interest costs may mean less money left over to pay for services. ( ABC: John Gunn ) "The rise in the Australian government's 10-year bond yield reflects a combination of rising yields globally and ongoing inflation concerns locally," Dr Oliver said. Longer-term bonds, like 10-year bonds, tend to influence the big banks' fixed rate mortgage products. Shorter-term bonds, like three-year bonds, and the Reserve Bank's cash rate influence variable rate mortgage products. Rising inflation concerns are lifting the interest rates on both longer-term and shorter-term bonds. The three-year bond, for example, saw its yield jump seven basis points or 0.07 percentage points to 4.73 per cent this afternoon. It's part of a global bond market sell-off, which is leading yields to multi-decade highs. Earlier today, Japan's 10-year government bond yield rose to 3 per cent, its highest since September 1996. The 10-Year British and US government bond yields have also surged today. The US government's debt burden has now surpassed $US40 trillion, and the market is not convinced the Trump administration is clear on how to reduce it. Last week, the US 30-year Treasury bond yield rose to 5.2 per cent for the first time in 19 years, when the global financial crisis was in full swing. Australian house prices have fallen for a fifth straight month as the impact of three Reserve Bank interest rate hikes and the government's tax changes affect confidence in the market. That's the return on lending money to the American government for three decades. And those ultra-long-term US borrowing costs have risen even further, to 5.28 per cent, for the first time since 2006. When a government's interest rate bill rises to such high levels, it shows people are worried about how debt and inflation will unfold.

events.title: Dubai to Damascus: Arada to build $7bn 'UAE-style' mixed-use project in Syria
events.summary: Property developer Arada has revealed plans to build a $7 billion "UAE-style" mixed-use real estate project in Syria. The new project in the west of Damascus will have 11,000 homes, including residential apartments, villas and townhouses, branded residences, 500 hotel rooms, and 1,000 serviced apartments, Arada said in a statement. There will also be two schools for 5,000 pupils, a 300-bed hospital, office space, commercial space, retail areas and government service buildings. “It’s a UAE-style fully integrated community, with all the amenities, social infrastructure, F&B, retail, plenty of greenery, sporting facilities and good quality homes ... a complete mixed-use development,” Ahmed Alkhoshaibi, group chief executive of Arada, told The National by the phone from Damascus. The project is to be built in phases over 10 years, with construction of homes and infrastructure to begin next year, he said. There is strong demand for “good quality homes” in Syria, driven by local residents and foreign citizens living abroad, he added. “You have the local current demand, which is very strong for good communities, but then you also have Syrians living outside, who want to invest, have a home or a holiday home, or for an investment in the country. So that demand will continue to grow," Mr Alkhoshaibi said. A public park spread across 700,000 square metres will also be built as part of the development, which will come up on four million square metres of land. Arada is working with the state-owned Syrian Sovereign Fund to deliver the project, and both entities are working to identify further sites for development across Syria, the company said. “Syria is at a pivotal moment in its history, and the scale of the opportunity to rebuild and invest in its future is significant,” said Arada executive vice chairman Prince Khaled bin Alwaleed . The new project will help create new jobs, develop local skills and support Syrian businesses, he added. The announcement of the new project comes after the US State Department last week removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, clearing a major obstacle to attracting new investment. It follows the repeal of the Caesar Act in December and the removal of economic sanctions by the European Union in May. The Syrian economy was devastated by the almost 14-year civil war, with severe damage to infrastructure and thousands fleeing the country to escape the conflict. Syria’s gross domestic product fell sharply during the war , and its gross national income per capita fell to just $830 in 2024. Reconstruction costs are estimated at $216 billion, according to the World Bank. “Syria welcomes businesses and companies from around the world, and this strategic partnership with Arada is a powerful demonstration of what that means in practice,” said Mohammed Al Khayyat, board member and chief executive of the real estate development sector at the Syrian Sovereign Fund. Arada, a joint venture between KBW Investments, a company controlled by Prince Khaled and Sharjah-based Basma Group, is continuing to expand in different markets, including Australia and the UK. The company now has a project pipeline valued at $42 billion across four markets and a portfolio of more than 66,000 homes spanning the UAE, the UK, Australia and Syria, according to the latest announcement. Other UAE developers are also looking to start projects in Syria. Emaar founder Mohamed Alabbar plans to invest as much as $18 billion in Syria in varied projects, as Damascus seeks to attract investment to rebuild its economy. The Dubai businessman is assessing projects worth between $5 billion and $7 billion on the Syrian coast and up to $11 billion in Damascus and its surroundings. The investment climate in Syria is positive as the country focuses on rebuilding its economy, Mr Alkhoshaibi said. “The amount of housing and social infrastructure that's required for a young population of 25 million is tremendous," he added. "So you need a lot of good developers. I expect a lot of developers to come into the market, especially after our announcement."

events.title: Debt-ridden developer at risk of collapse unless it secures $20m tonight
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bathla Group's collapse may be imminent as funding deadline brought forward Topic: Housing Construction Industry Bathla Group has been teetering on the brink of collapse. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) Hopes for an eleventh-hour cash injection into the crumbling Bathla Group are fading fast as some lenders take matters into their own hands. The administrators have brought forward a deadline to the end of Tuesday to see if the business has any chance of survival. Administrators are preparing to shut down the company imminently if funding cannot be secured. Hopes for crumbling property developer Bathla Group are deteriorating fast as a crucial deadline was brought forward while some lenders took action into their own hands. Bathla's administrator, Teneo, has said it is preparing to shut down the company by the end of the day as hopes of securing $20 million in emergency funding fade away. The realisation came after a meeting with lenders on Monday night failed to secure the commitment needed. Teneo senior managing director Stephen Longley told Nine's Today Show: "We'll start planning at the end of the day for the wind down of the business," and said the situation was "very dire". Stephen Longley implored someone to step forward to save the business at a press conference on Monday. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) "We're running out of hope for a holistic solution to finish the 45 construction projects," he said. "We've had intensive discussions with lenders, but I don't think we're going to get enough funding in place." Mr Longley's latest comments were more pessimistic than yesterday, when he told ABC's The Business that he remained hopeful of securing a last-minute lifeline from lenders. He also said, at a press conference on Monday, the property firm had "no cash", but could still complete at least 45 construction projects if it received more funding. Some of Bathla's 350 staff have not been paid for eight weeks while the developer has accumulated debts exceeding $3.2 billion. Bathla Group has failed to secure a lifeline. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) Bathla's administration has left the fate of 200 building projects across NSW in jeopardy, with about 2,000 homes under construction and another 13,000 in its development pipeline. Some private credit lenders have taken control of individual worksites and will be responsible for delivering particular projects. The ABC understands a 312-apartment block development in Pemulwuy in Sydney's west is going ahead after the lender, PAG, made a commitment to continue paying contractors directly. A manufacturing contractor who provided his first name, Moqvul, said that PAG had told him not to worry and continue working on the Pemulwuy site. Mustafa, the owner of a kitchen joinery business, told the ABC he had received a written commitment from PAG, but it did not extend to any other Bathla sites. He was also unsure what it meant for outstanding bills that his business was owed. Contractors spoke to the ABC after a crisis meeting with lender PAG at a site in Pemulwuy on Tuesday. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) "No-one is giving us any clear image of where we are heading," Mustafa said. "We are stressed. We owe the ATO, we owe the suppliers, we owe the workers." Another contractor, Charbel, said the situation "didn't look good" and said he had four kids and was owed "a fair bit" of money from Bathla. Administrators had tried tapping existing lenders for extra funds and late last week asked the New South Wales government for a $20 million lifeline to keep the business afloat . However, the state government refused to offer any bailout money. Bathla Group has taken at least 1,000 deposits off customers, administrators have said. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) Teneo also said it had borrowed $1 million from its own head office so Bathla Group could afford to pay for vehicle registrations, petrol and "just to keep the lights on". Its situation has also left questions around how home buyers will be impacted, including deposits. Mr Longley said on Monday as many as 1,000 deposits could have been paid to the developer, and that some of those may have been used. "Some of the contracts allow the deposits to be used by the business, deposits have been used as the contracts allow," he said. events.title: How misconceptions and woeful PR allowed Musk to shred USAID so easily | Jeremiah A Carew
events.summary: How misconceptions and woeful PR allowed Musk to shred USAID so easily A year on from the purge, with thousands of jobs cut and billions in foreign aid lost, a former leader reflects on the sorry saga – and why it would never happen to Nasa A year has passed since I and thousands of colleagues lost our jobs at USAID . Asking myself “Why us?” I have come to the conclusion that the American public had very little idea of what we were doing and why. Doge, the “department of government efficiency” , began its work in January 2025, with USAID as its first target, in a reckless campaign that even Elon Musk has said he would not repeat . At that moment of chaos, Americans lacked the knowledge that could contradict the false narrative presented by Musk , who called the agency a “criminal organisation” and “a viper’s nest of radical left-marxists who hate America”. But what if Doge had eliminated Nasa , not USAID? Such a scenario seems highly implausible. Despite the rise of private space companies, Nasa remains an icon of national prestige, with broad bipartisan congressional support. How many kids want to be astronauts when they grow up? I sure did. And that’s because Nasa has spent decades carefully communicating its results and cultivating its image with the public. In contrast, USAID is not well known or understood. One expert on USAID’s brand noted that the agency’s handclasp emblem and the tagline “from the American people” were “well known in the developing world, even if not well known in Washington”. How much worse is that brand recognition in middle America? Misunderstandings around foreign aid abound. In March 2025, a Kaiser Family Foundation survey reported : “Nearly nine in 10 (86%) adults overestimate the share of the federal budget spent on foreign aid, saying on average that the US spends about a quarter (26%) of its budget on foreign aid.” In fact, about 1% of the federal budget goes on foreign aid. Unfortunately, that lack of recognition and those gross misunderstandings were key factors in USAID’s elimination. It may never be resurrected, but the question remains important: what could future foreign assistance learn from Nasa’s approach to public communications, to ensure broad public understanding and support? Without a doubt, stories were there to be told. In Colombia, where I was deputy director of the largest USAID mission in the hemisphere from 2021 to 2025, we contributed to solving major regional challenges. We helped tens of thousands of Venezuelans take advantage of generous Colombian migration policies by processing legal residency cards, training them for jobs and establishing healthcare access. That meant they could stay in Colombia legally, rather than add to the thousands of migrants trying to enter the US. We guaranteed hundreds of millions of dollars in loans Colombian banks made to new businesses. These businesses promoted tropical forest products such as açaí to keep the Amazon’s trees standing. Other loans helped poor farmers build businesses with legal crops instead of coca, which is turned into cocaine, causing addiction and death in the US and Europe. These loan-guarantee programmes cost the US government pennies on the dollar to reduce risk so that Colombian banks would extend their loans to new, unfamiliar businesses. And after Colombia’s government successfully negotiated a historic peace accord in 2016, ending 50 years of civil conflict, USAID was the largest donor to help them implement it. Among many things, that meant helping prosecutors gather testimony from thousands of victims of violence so the truth could be told and justice done. When fighters turned in their guns to lead peaceful lives, efforts such as ours helped Colombians achieve some form of reconciliation and turn the page. These are not simple stories to tell. As these examples illustrate, real development work is not handing out goodies for a photo op. It is making strategic nudges to a country’s own efforts to do the things that solve global challenges – illegal migration, climate breakdown, illegal drugs and yes, world peace – while reflecting its national interest. Telling USAID’s story to the American public accurately – describing projects far from home, in complex and unfamiliar foreign contexts – is challenging. Yet faced with its own challenges in communicating technically complex scientific work performed thousands of miles from home, Nasa succeeded where USAID failed. The 2014 book Marketing the Moon, by David Meerman Scott and Richard Jurek, focuses on the Apollo programme, when 94% of American televisions were tuned to the first lunar landing. They argue that “without strong public support abetted by high-profile, enthusiastic public relations, the entire achievement and its funding would have been unthinkable”. Echoes of these strategies are still seen, and Nasa still excels in communicating with the public.

events.title: Vance reaches out to Jewish Republicans in Vegas speech
events.summary: Vice President Vance on Monday offered an olive branch to Jewish Republicans who have grown wary of his views toward Israel. During a closed-door appearance before the Republican Jewish Coalition at the Venetian hotel in Las Vegas, Vance called Israel "extremely important to America's national security" and condemned rising antisemitism. Why it matters: Vance's appearance at the meeting is the latest indication that he's trying to repair ties with a powerful but skeptical constituency within the GOP ahead of an expected bid for president in 2028. In a 30-minute Q&A session with former Minnesota Sen. Norm Coleman, Vance recalled discussing antisemitism with the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk, who he said shared his view that "Jew hatred is corrosive to the soul." Vance blamed some of the recent rise in antisemitism on immigration, claiming that "a lot" of it was "coming from these Third World immigrants importing these ancient ethnic hatreds." "If you want to bring ethnic hatreds with you, don't bother coming to the United States," Vance said. He added that there was "a much deeper cultural symbiosis and harmony" to the U.S. relationship with nations such as the United Kingdom and Israel compared to other allies. The background: Tensions between Vance and the pro-Israel conservatives have been growing for months. During the lead-up to the Iran war, Vance privately expressed a belief that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had given overly rosy projections about how U.S. military action would play out. Vance confronted Netanyahu over those predictions after the war began. After helping broker a U.S.-Iran deal — which quickly fell apart — Vance warned the Israelis to stand down in their opposition, reminding them of their reliance on U.S. support. During a mid-July interview with podcaster Joe Rogan, Vance said he knew "beyond a shadow of a doubt" that people within Israel's government were trying to prescribe U.S.-Iran diplomacy because "they want to continue the military campaign." Vance's interview with Rogan drew pushback from pro-Israel conservatives, including podcaster Ben Shapiro. Netanyahu confronted Vance over his criticisms of Israel's government in a meeting later that month. Behind the scenes: Jewish Republicans have long expressed discomfort over Vance's relationship with podcaster Tucker Carlson, who has faced accusations of antisemitism. During his appearance at the RJC, Vance was asked about how the party should deal with right-of-center podcasters who have been critical of Israel, including Carlson, Rogan, Megyn Kelly and Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes. Vance responded that Republicans should aggressively engage with such personalities and make the case for Israel. He didn't address his relationship with Carlson, but defended Rogan and criticized Fuentes, who Vance said "has nothing but hate in his heart." State of play: Earlier Monday, Vance campaigned in Michigan, where he accused progressive Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of being more sympathetic toward the attacker of a synagogue than for its Jewish victims. The intrigue: Vance's appearance at RJC highlights a centerpiece of his pre-2028 strategy — appearing before audiences that aren't reflexively supportive . During his recent book tour, Vance sparred with liberal-leaning personalities such as Bill Maher and the hosts of "The View."

events.title: Materials to rebuild homes after disaster rise by 70pc in five years, report finds
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Costs of building a home rise by almost 30 per cent in five years, Insurance Council of Australia finds Topic: Housing Construction Industry Between 2022 and 2026, insurers received 400,000 claims to repair or rebuild homes damaged in declared events. The cost to build a home in Australia has risen almost 30 per cent in five years, with the price of some construction materials going up by as much as 70 per cent, according to a new report. Prices have risen most steeply in Queensland and northern Australia, where it now costs 44 per cent more to build a home than it did in 2021, the report from the Insurance Council of Australia found. Between 2022 and 2026, insurers received 400,000 claims to repair or rebuild homes damaged in declared events, costing $11.3 billion. Materials most needed after a natural disaster have gone up in cost the most, with roof tiles up more than 70 per cent — more than three times the rate of inflation — and windows, plasterboard and concrete prices increasing upwards of 37 per cent. In the past five years, in Queensland alone, insurers have repaired or replaced more than 240,000 homes. ( ABC News: Sophie Johnson ) Insurance Council Australia (ICA) chief executive Andrew Hall said inflation was driving up costs, and people's premiums with it. "In states like Queensland, where quite often it's severe storms that impact a home, those things that need replacing immediately are the things that are costing the most, that all goes into the calculation when we're looking at the cost of an insurance premium," he said. Meanwhile, as extreme weather events become more frequent and severe, Australia is repairing nearly as many homes as it is building new ones. In 2025, declared events damaged 145,392 homes. Nationally, 172,657 new homes were built. In the past five years, in Queensland alone, insurers have repaired or replaced more than 240,000 homes. Andrew Hall says the insurance sector is competing for the same workers and materials as builders to repair damaged houses. ( ABC News: Craig Hansen ) "These are homes that are already existing which means we're competing with the same sector that's trying to deliver new homes to meet the housing challenges," Mr Hall said. It's set up a "double whammy" where insurers vie with builders for materials and trades, he said. Queenslanders warned about 'disaster chasers' targeting storm-hit homeowners Home owners in storm-hit parts of Queensland are being warned about “disaster chasers” targeting vulnerable residents. "Not only are we trying to meet the affordability and accessibility challenge, we're at the same time competing for the same builders and materials to repair existing housing stock." The report recommends Australia builds more resilient homes, and stop homes being built in high-risk areas. Cyclone Jasper turned Kathy Pitt's house into a skeleton. It took $160,000 from her superannuation and about $70,000 government grants to get the uninsured owner her Holloways Beach home back, and there's still work to be done. Kathy Pitt says to date it has cost about $230,000 to repair her house after Cyclone Jasper. ( ABC News: Brendan Mounter ) "I suppose I didn't believe but I just had to pay it off in some way and lucky I had that money," she said. "I put it off … and then you put it off a bit longer and it costs even more." Ms Pitt said being in Far North Queensland, there are fewer trades to choose from so it was hard to get more than one quote, and materials and labour was more expensive. Even with the cost of repairs without insurance, Ms Pitt said premiums are "too prohibitive" for her to be insured after being quoted about $12,000. Far North Queensland owner-operator Matt Hart says it is tough to have to pass the cost onto customers. ( ABC News: Brendan Mounter ) Far North Queensland builder Matt Hart said there was little he could do to lower costs. "Unfortunately, the cost of materials is just something we have to pass on to the consumer and the client," he said. "I can't do anything about materials, but I can do something about the hourly rate and labour." "Future-proofed" homes would stop resources for new buildings being diverted for repairs, Paula Jarzabkowski, Professor in Strategic Management at the University of Queensland said. Instead of rebuilding "like for like", repairs need to make a home safer and more likely to withstand severe weather, she added. Paula Jarzabkowski says there needs to be a focus on building future-proofed homes.
